newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defends Lake and Berger on stock holdings.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defends Lake and Berger on stock holdings.

text.p: President Bill Clinton defended top national security aides Anthony Lake and Samuel Berger on Friday in the face of investigations into their stock holdings, saying they had done nothing "disqualifying."

The Justice Department is investigating whether Lake, as Clinton's national security adviser, and Berger, as Lake's deputy, had conflicts of interest because they failed to take timely action on orders to sell off their personal holdings in energy stocks.
Clinton has nominated Lake as his new director of central intelligence and has appointed Berger as Lake's successor.

At a news conference Clinton said he was aware of the questions about their investments but, based on the advice of White House counsel Jack Quinn, decided to go ahead with their appointments, "because I am convinced that nothing they did was in any way disqualifying."
Lake's nomination requires Senate confirmation. Berger's appointment does not. White House aides did not believe the disclosures posed any problem for the two officials.
Officials said Lake was advised in 1993 by the counsel's office that he should sell various energy stocks in his personal portfolio.

Lake agreed and told investigators he thought his secretary told his broker to sell them. But in 1995 a review by the White House counsel's office of his 1994 financial disclosure forms showed he still owned the stocks. He then sold them.
Berger's case was similar. In 1993 his financial disclosure form listed 1,500 Amoco oil company shares were held for many years in a trust established by his wife's grandfather.
White House legal advisers told him in early 1994 the holdings represented a potential conflict and that he should sell, but Berger was sceptical, officials said.

He was told he had to sell because he was involved in policy decisions on whether to maintain sanctions on Iraq and Libya. Berger ultimately agreed to sell but said he forgot about the matter and never did until he was reminded of it in June 1995.
He reportedly sold the shares for $90,350. If he had sold them when originally told to do so, they would have brought $71,000.
Clinton said he went ahead with the Lake and Berger selections even though the Justice Department probe was not completed, because "the work of the people has to go forward."

"There's nothing there that has not been disclosed, to the best of my knowledge," Clinton said. "And I made a decision based on the advice of my counsel that the best people that I wanted to appoint could, in fact, be appointed."

Broadly speaking, Clinton said, "everybody's going to make some mistakes," and the partisan atmosphere in Washington that leads to political attacks and investigation has dissuaded many talented people from considering public service.
"The question is, does the mistake amount to a violation of law? Does it amount to a dereliction of duty? Does it amount to some dark attempt to undermine the public interest?" he said.

He said the law authorising creation of independent counsels to conduct freewheeling investigations, a number of which are pursuing probes of his administration and finances from years ago, should be assessed, but by people "who aren't so personally involved in it."
